text: Every winter, the village of Kestrel put one lantern on the hill.
Not for the living. For whoever was still walking home.
Old Mira had carried it up for forty-one years.
Forty-one winters. The same seven hundred steps.
The rule was simple. Light it before dark, and never look back down.
Nobody living remembered who made the rule.
The winter Mira turned eighty, the snow came early.
It buried the path by noon, and the markers by three.
She went up anyway, with the lantern held under her coat.
Halfway, the wind found the flame and took it.
And in the dark, she heard the thing the rule was for.
Footsteps. Below her. Climbing.
Mira did not look back. She had promised, sixty years ago.
She struck a match. The wind ate it.
She struck another, and another, until her hands would not close.
The footsteps stopped, one step behind her.
And a voice she had not heard since she was a girl said her name.
Mira turned around.
There was nobody on the stairs. Only snow, and her own tracks, going up.
And the lantern in her hands was burning.
She never learned who lit it.
But she carried it to the top, and set it down, and walked home.
In Kestrel they still put a lantern on the hill each winter.
They still tell you not to look back. They no longer tell you why.
